phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] plus close front [i], a hissing opening that identifies the 'woman' element.
Rounded [w] plus open [a], the glide linking cihua- 'woman' to the snake element.
Voiceless velar stop [k] plus long back rounded [oː]; c before back vowels is /k/ in Classical Nahuatl.
Long open [aː] plus lateral affricate [tɬ]; final -tl is a single released sound.

pronunciation.approximation: 'see-wah-KOH-ahtl' — the first vowel is short, the 'c' is a hard 'k,' and the final -tl is one crisp tongue-stop.

kin.label: Title and office
kin.form: Cihuacōātl was also the title of a high-ranking Mexica official, 'Woman-Snake,' the second voice of the ruler

kin.label: Modern spelling
kin.form: Cihuacoatl, the conventional form that drops the macrons

pronunciation.note: The name is a transparent compound of cihuātl ('woman') and cōātl ('snake'). The first vowel (i) is short; the long vowel the written compound leaves unmarked is the ā of cihuātl, shortened in the compound (compound-shortening). The same word was used as a political title, the Cihuacōātl or 'Woman-Snake,' a high official of the Mexica state. In religion, Cihuacōātl is a powerful goddess of childbirth, maternity, and the dangers that attend both. Tier 1: the macrons preserve vowel length, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Snake Woman
domains.subtitle: Childbirth, Midwifery, and the Fate of Mothers
domains.lead: Cihuacōātl is the divine midwife and the spectral woman who haunts the crossroads. In one aspect she protects women in labor; in another she wanders at night weeping for children who died unbaptized into life. She embodies the dangerous threshold between pregnancy and birth, life and death, the domestic hearth and the wild road.

cards.name: Goddess of Childbirth
cards.desc: She aids women in labor and receives the afterbirth; midwives call upon her and make offerings.

cards.name: Protector of Midwives
cards.desc: The tēntitl 'midwife' served as her human representative; birthing rituals invoked her power.

cards.name: The Weeping Woman
cards.desc: La Llorona, the wailing specter of crossroads and waterways, descends partly from Cihuacōātl lore.

cards.name: Fate and Threshold
cards.desc: She governs the dangerous moment when a new life crosses from the spirit world into the body.

mythology.lead: Cihuacōātl's mythology is preserved in the birth rituals recorded by Sahagún and in the widespread Mexican legend of the weeping woman. She is both a beneficent guardian and a terrifying ghost, a duality that reflects the high mortality of childbirth in the pre-modern world.

myths.title: The Midwives’ Prayer
myths.text: Sahagún’s informants describe how the midwife received the newborn as a captive taken in sacred battle: the child, they said, had been chosen in the land of the dead by the gods and delivered into the midwife’s hands. She addressed the infant as a warrior arriving from the sky, invoked the divine protectresses of the birthing chamber — among them Cihuacōātl — cut the umbilicus over an open vessel, and buried the afterbirth in the corner of the house as an offering. The child was bathed, named, and ritually presented to the gods; the cord of a girl child was buried by the hearth, that of a boy by the fields, fixing each life to its future work. Cihuacōātl’s presence ensured the dangerous passage from womb to world ended in life rather than death (Florentine Codex, Book VI). The ritual means birth was classified as war: the mother a battlefield, the midwife a commander, and the goddess the power holding the door.

myths.title: The Cihuapipiltin and the Crossroads
myths.text: Women who died in childbirth — above all in a first labor — were believed to become cihuāpīpiltin, “noble women,” spirits of enormous and ambivalent power. They wandered at night dressed in white, faces chalked, hair loose, weeping at crossroads and waterways for the children they had lost; they could seize or strike men who mocked them, appear as omens of war, and visit fathers in dreams. Yet the same powers defended their communities: the spirits of women dead in childbirth were counted among the fierce dead who carried the sun from noon to setting, soldiers in the sky’s war. Over centuries this figure merged with Spanish colonial ghost-lore to produce La Llorona, the weeping woman of Mexican folklore. The transformation means a goddess of childbirth survived conquest by becoming a ghost — the cult suppressed, the grief irrepressible.

myths.title: The Cihuacōātl of Tenochtitlan
myths.text: The name was also the second-highest office of the Mexica state: Cihuacōātl, “Woman-Snake,” counselor and executor of the ruler’s will. Diego Durán and the Florentine Codex describe the office as “speaker of the city,” sometimes rendered vice-ruler, charged with internal order — the courts, the marketplace, the tribute rolls — while the tlātoāni managed war and diplomacy. Tlācaelel, the great architect of the Aztec state under Itzcōātl and Motēuczōma, held the title for decades and is credited with rebuilding the whole imperial ideology. That the state’s chief magistrate bore a goddess’s name — and a goddess of childbirth at that — suggests the office carried sacred as well as administrative authority: the state, like the birthing chamber, governed a threshold where death stood close by.

myths.title: The Woman Who Cried in the Night
myths.text: When the strangers from the east were coming, omens walked the land — and among them, the ancient ones. The Florentine Codex (Book 12) records that in the tenth year before the strangers’ arrival a woman’s voice was heard crying in the night: “My children, my children, we are lost! Where shall I take you? We are lost, we are doomed!” — the cry of a cihuāteōtl, one of the divine women who had died in childbirth, mourning the world that was ending. The same book lists the comet, the burning temple of Huitzilopochtli, and the mirror that showed the armies marching. Read against her older cult, the wailing woman of the omens is Cihuacōātl herself turned prophetess of catastrophe. The myth means the goddess of birth had become the goddess of ending: the same threshold, walked the other way.

lore.syncretism: Cihuacōātl merges in popular memory with La Llorona, the weeping woman of crossroads and rivers, and with the Virgin Mary in her sorrowful or protective aspects. The cihuapipiltin spirits share traits with the Celtic-Spanish banshee and with other worldwide figures of the woman who died in childbirth. In Nahuatl religion she is closely related to Cōātlīcue and Tlāltēcuhtli, forming a cluster of serpent-and-earth maternal powers.
lore.culturalLegacy: Cihuacōātl survives most visibly in La Llorona, a figure known throughout Mexico and the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. The weeping woman at the water's edge, mourning children lost to drowning, violence, or history, carries the ancient goddess into contemporary song, film, and political allegory. Feminist and Chicana writers have reclaimed both Cihuacōātl and La Llorona as symbols of maternal grief, female autonomy, and the suppressed voices of indigenous women.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Cihuacōātl lives at the threshold. She is the goddess you call when the door between life and death is swinging open and a child is trying to pass through. For most of human history, that door was wider than it is now; many women and infants did not survive the crossing. Cihuacōātl is the divine witness to that grief.

Her later form as La Llorona shows how ancient goddesses become ghosts, and how ghosts become moral lessons. But beneath the cautionary tale is something older and more tender: the recognition that birth is a battle, that mothers are warriors, and that some losses echo forever along the roads and rivers. To speak her name with the long vowels restored is to remember that this was once a goddess, not merely a bogey.

lore.archaeology: Cihuacōātl is not represented by a single monumental sculpture comparable to Cōātlīcue, but her presence is documented in the birth rituals recorded by Sahagún, in ceramic figurines of women in childbirth, and in the large corpus of Nahuatl ritual speech preserved in colonial manuscripts. Cross-cultural parallels with Maya childbirth deities and with colonial-period ex-votos suggest a long history of female-divine assistance at birth in Mesoamerica.
